title: Ubaid Mesopotamia
subtitle: 6500–3800 BC · The Pottery Neolithic of the North and the Rise of the Ubaid Culture in the Southern Marshes

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The pottery Neolithic of the north — Hassuna, Samarra and Halaf — and the rise of the Ubaid culture in the southern marshes and its spread across the whole basin

entries.label: Hassuna — the first villages of the northern plain
entries.hint: On the rain-fed steppe of the upper Tigris and the Sinjar plain, the earliest fully agricultural villages of Mesopotamia formed — small clusters of rectangular multi-room mudbrick houses with courtyards, grain bins and bread ovens, farming barley and emmer and herding sheep and goats. The specialised onager-hunting outpost at Umm Dabaghiyah shows the range of the economy. Coarse cooking pots and simple painted or incised wares mark the horizon.
entries.note: Type site excavated by Seton Lloyd & Fuad Safar for the Iraqi Directorate of Antiquities, 'Tell Hassuna' (1945, JNES); Umm Dabaghiyah by Diana Kirkbride (1971–75); Yarim Tepe I by the Soviet expedition of Merpert & Munchaev.

entries.label: Samarra — farming crosses the dry line
entries.loc: Tell es-Sawwan, on the Tigris below Samarra
entries.hint: Along the middle Tigris, at the edge of where rain-fed farming is possible, Samarran communities pushed agriculture into drier land by cutting simple canals from the river — the first irrigation in Mesopotamia. Tell es-Sawwan was a substantial planted village with T-shaped houses, alabaster figurines and statuettes in its graves, and a defensive ditch. Its fine painted pottery, with dancing women, fish and scorpions swirling around the interior, was carried far beyond the Samarra zone.
entries.note: Pottery first recognised by Ernst Herzfeld at Samarra (1911–13); Tell es-Sawwan excavated by the Iraqi Directorate of Antiquities (El-Wailly & Abu es-Soof, 1964–71); Choga Mami by Joan Oates (1967–68), who defined the 'Samarra' irrigation model.

entries.label: Halaf — the painted-pottery north
entries.hint: Across northern Mesopotamia and into Syria and southeast Anatolia, Halaf communities lived in villages of round domed houses (tholoi) and produced the most technically and artistically accomplished painted pottery of the ancient Near East — thin-walled, lustrous, polychrome, and traded as a prestige good over hundreds of kilometres. No site dominates the others and no palaces or central stores appear: the Halaf north looks like a network of roughly equal communities, not a hierarchy.
entries.note: Tell Halaf excavated by Max von Oppenheim (1911–13, 1927–29); Arpachiyah by Max Mallowan & J. C. Rose (1933); modern synthesis in Stuart Campbell and in Akkermans & Schwartz, 'The Archaeology of Syria' (2003).

entries.label: The first settlement of the southern marshes
entries.hint: At the head of the Gulf, on levees and turtlebacks amid the marshes, the earliest known settlers of the southern alluvium built small villages with painted pottery close in style to Samarra's. Eridu's deepest levels begin a temple sequence rebuilt on the same spot for two thousand years; Tell el-Oueili has the oldest alluvial deposits yet found. Whether earlier villages lie buried under metres of river silt and a risen water table is the unanswered 'Ubaid problem'.
entries.note: Eridu excavated by Fuad Safar, Seton Lloyd & Mohammad Ali Mustafa (1946–49), published as 'Eridu' (1981); Tell el-Oueili by the French mission under Jean-Louis Huot (1976–89).

entries.label: The mature Ubaid of the south
entries.hint: The southern culture that gives the whole period its name spread across the alluvium — Ur, Uruk, al-Ubaid, Tell el-Oueili — with a recurring package: the tripartite house and temple plan, greenish painted pottery giving way to plain mass-produced bowls, the bent clay 'sickle' of fired earth, and a slow but steady growth in the number and size of settlements. Society shows differences of wealth and role but no kings and no walled centres.
entries.note: Al-Ubaid excavated by H. R. Hall & Leonard Woolley (1919, 1923–24); the 'Ubaid' as a period defined at the 1930 Baghdad conference; synthesis in Carter & Philip (eds.), 'Beyond the Ubaid' (2010).

entries.label: The first pan-Mesopotamian horizon
entries.hint: Ubaid pottery, the tripartite building and the stamp seal spread north over the former Halaf zone — Tepe Gawra, Tell Zeidan on the Euphrates, sites in the Khabur and up to the Taurus — and down the Arabian shore of the Gulf. For the first time a single material culture linked the whole of Mesopotamia, north and south, and its edges. Whether this was migration, emulation or trade is still argued; the result was a shared world.
entries.note: Tepe Gawra excavated by E. A. Speiser & Charles Bache (1927–38); Tell Zeidan by Gil Stein (2008–11); the expansion debated across the essays in Carter & Philip (eds.), 'Beyond the Ubaid' (2010).

entries.label: The temple towns and the eve of the city
entries.hint: By the end of the period the largest southern sites were true towns of ten hectares or more — Eridu with its mudbrick platform temple, Tell Abada in the Hamrin with its big central house, Kheit Qasim. A two-tier pattern of larger and smaller settlements appears, and the temple stands out as the community's monumental focus. The shift into the Uruk period that follows is gradual, with no break in occupation at the main sites.
entries.note: Eridu Temple sequence in Safar, Lloyd & Mustafa, 'Eridu' (1981); Tell Abada by Sabah Abboud Jasim, 'The Ubaid Period in Iraq' (1985); regional synthesis in Susan Pollock, 'Ancient Mesopotamia' (1999).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The scarce evidence for organised violence — the ditch and wall of Tell es-Sawwan, burnt villages, and the near-absence of war from Ubaid art

entries.label: The ditch and wall of Tell es-Sawwan
entries.hint: The Samarran village of Tell es-Sawwan was ringed by a ditch three metres deep cut into virgin soil and, on the river side, a buttressed mudbrick wall — the earliest defensive circuit known in Mesopotamia. Whether it guarded stored grain and irrigated land against raiders, or against the Tigris in flood, is disputed; either way it marks a community with something worth enclosing.
entries.note: Iraqi Directorate of Antiquities excavations (El-Wailly & Abu es-Soof, 'Excavations at Tell es-Sawwan', Sumer 1965); defensive interpretation reviewed in Roger Matthews, 'The Archaeology of Mesopotamia' (2003).

entries.label: Burnt houses in the Hassuna–Halaf north
entries.hint: Several northern villages preserve houses destroyed by fierce fires — most famously the 'Burnt Village' at Tell Sabi Abyad on the Balikh, whose blaze baked and preserved a store of clay sealings. Whether such fires were accidents, ritual closings or the marks of raiding cannot usually be told, but they show that village life was not without violent episodes.
entries.note: Yarim Tepe fire levels in Merpert & Munchaev's reports; the Sabi Abyad 'Burnt Village' in Peter Akkermans (ed.), 'Tell Sabi Abyad' (1996) and Akkermans & Duistermaat on its sealings.

entries.label: The near-absence of war from Ubaid life
entries.hint: Set against the later Uruk and Early Dynastic record — bound prisoners, smiting scenes, city walls, standing armies — Ubaid material culture is strikingly unmartial. Maces and clay sling-bullets occur, but fortified sites are rare and there is no iconography of battle or captives. Many archaeologists read this, with the shallow gradient of Ubaid wealth and status, as a society not yet organised for war.
entries.note: Argument developed in Gil Stein, 'Economy, Ritual, and Power in Ubaid Mesopotamia' (1994) and in the settlement analyses collected in Carter & Philip (eds.), 'Beyond the Ubaid' (2010).

entries.label: Choga Mami and the contested edge of irrigation
entries.hint: On the Mandali fan, where canal farming met the Zagros piedmont and its herding populations, the Samarran site of Choga Mami was entered through a buttressed gateway tower and lay beside some of the oldest traceable irrigation channels in the world. The combination — new canals, new land, a guarded entrance — hints at friction along the frontier between farmers and their neighbours.
entries.note: Choga Mami excavated by Joan Oates (1967–68), 'Choga Mami 1967–68: A Preliminary Report' (Iraq 1969); irrigation channels discussed in Oates & Oates, 'The Rise of Civilization' (1976).
